content: Overactive bladder syndrome (OAB) is a prevalent condition that significantly diminishes quality of life. It is characterized by symptoms such as urinary urgency, with or without urge incontinence, increased frequency of urination, and nocturia. Intravesical botulinum toxin injections are increasingly being utilized as a treatment option for individuals with severe OAB that does not respond to standard management strategies. A growing body of evidence supports the use of this intervention, indicating that it is effective, well-tolerated, and safe. This review represents a substantial update to a prior review conducted in 2007. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy of intravesical botulinum toxin injections compared to other treatments for both neurogenic and idiopathic OAB in adults. Specific hypotheses addressed included whether botulinum toxin injections were superior to placebo or no treatment, whether they were more effective than pharmacological or non-pharmacological interventions, whether higher doses were more effective than lower doses, whether combining botulinum toxin with other treatments was superior to using other treatments alone, whether one formulation of botulinum toxin was superior to another, and whether different injection techniques yielded different outcomes. The search for relevant studies was conducted using the Cochrane Incontinence Group Specialised Trials Register, which includes trials identified from databases such as MEDLINE, CINAHL, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), as well as through handsearching journals and conference proceedings. The search was performed on February 23, 2010, and no restrictions were applied to the search criteria. Additionally, reference lists of selected trials and relevant review articles were examined. The review included all randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials involving adults with OAB, where at least one treatment arm involved intravesical botulinum toxin injections. Participants included those with neurogenic OAB or idiopathic OAB, with or without stress incontinence. Comparison interventions included no treatment, placebo, lifestyle modifications, bladder retraining, pharmacological therapies, surgical interventions, bladder instillation techniques, neuromodulation, and various types, doses, and injection techniques of botulinum toxin. Binary outcomes were analyzed using relative risk, while continuous outcomes were assessed using mean differences. Due to variability in study designs and outcome measures, data synthesis across studies was limited. Standard deviations were calculated from P values when necessary, following the methodology outlined in the Cochrane Handbook of Systematic Reviews of Interventions. Data were presented in tabular form where possible, and results were extracted directly from trial reports when necessary. In cases where multiple publications reported on the same study, the data were treated as a single source. A total of 19 studies met the inclusion criteria. Most of these studies involved patients with neurogenic OAB, although some included individuals with idiopathic OAB. Across all studies, botulinum toxin demonstrated superior efficacy compared to placebo. Lower doses of botulinum toxin (100 to 150 units) were effective, but higher doses (300 units) appeared to provide greater and longer-lasting benefits, albeit with an increased risk of side effects. Suburothelial injection was found to be as effective as intradetrusor injection. The therapeutic effects of botulinum toxin lasted for several months and were influenced by the dose and type of toxin used. Importantly, patients who received repeated injections did not appear to develop resistance to the treatment. Botulinum toxin also showed greater efficacy compared to intravesical resiniferatoxin. While the treatment was generally safe, one study was discontinued due to an unacceptably high rate of urinary retention. In conclusion, intravesical botulinum toxin appears to be an effective treatment for refractory OAB symptoms. However, there is limited controlled trial data comparing its benefits and safety to other interventions or placebo. Further high-quality research is needed to establish long-term outcomes, safety profiles, and the optimal dosing regimen for botulinum toxin in the management of OAB.
